source_text:
ἐν τῷ γὰρ εἰπεῖν· καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεός· ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν, ζήτημα ἐνέβαλε νοῆσαι ἡμᾶς, πρὸς τίνα ἔλεγε τὸ ποιήσωμεν· εἰπὼν γὰρ· καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεός· ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον, ἐπήγαγε λέγων· καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ ἐποίησεν
αὐτὸν, ἄρρεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησε αὐτούς. Ἡ οὖν τοῦ ποιήσωμεν σημασία τὸ εἶναι πρόσωπον συνδημιουργὸν σημαίνει καὶ συνισοπροσήγορον εἰσάγει. Ὡς γὰρ Θεὸς ὁ Πατήρ ἐστιν ὁ εἰπών· ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον, οὕτω Θεός ἐστι καὶ πρὸς ὃν τὸ ποιήσωμεν εἴρηκε, μιᾶς οὔσης τῆς τῶν ἀμφοτέρων προσώπων θεότητος, τοῦ τε εἰπόντος· ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν, καὶ τοῦ ποιήσαντος τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Τὸ γὰρ ποιήσωμεν τὸ πανάγιον καὶ ἀπαράλλακτον τῆς τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ θεότητος παρίστησιν ἡ φωνή· ἡ γὰρ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰκὼν ἁπλῆ καὶ ἀσύνθετός ἐστι, πῦρ οὖσα τῇ φύσει.
thought_title: The plural 'let us make' reveals a co-creator
orientation: Eustathius is answering the philosopher's question about whom God addressed in Genesis 1:26, arguing that the plural verb introduces a co-creating person.
pass_a_gloss: For in the saying: 'And God said: let us make a human being in our image and in likeness,' [he] threw in a question [for] us to understand, to whom he was saying the 'let us make.' For having said: 'And God said: let us make a human being,' he brought on saying: 'And God made the human being, in God's image he made him, male and female he made them.' The meaning therefore of the 'let us make' signifies the being [of] a co-creator person and introduces [one] of equal address. For as God the Father is the one having said: 'let us make a human being,' so God is also [the one] to whom he said the 'let us make,' the deity of both persons being one, both of the one having said: 'let us make a human being in our image and in likeness,' and of the one having made the human being. For the 'let us make' presents the all-holy and unvarying deity of the Father and Son, the voice [does]; for the image of God is simple and uncompounded, being light in nature.

choices.why: The rare compound means someone addressed on the same footing; 'equal address' keeps the co-equal force without importing a later trinitarian term.
The adjective means 'not differing' or 'invariable'; 'unvarying' fits the context of the shared deity of Father and Son.
The verb means 'exhibits' or 'displays'; 'presents' keeps the demonstrative force of the voice showing the deity.
The verb is vivid and active; 'threw in' preserves the sense that the text itself poses the question for the reader.

bible_refs.note: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεός· ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν
καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, κατ' εἰκόνα Θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν, ἄρρεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησε αὐτούς

pass_b_english: For by saying, “And God said, ‘Let us make a human being in our image and in our likeness’” (Genesis 1:26), the text throws in a question for us to understand: to whom was he saying “let us make”? After saying, “And God said, ‘Let us make a human being,’” it goes on to say, “And God made the human being; in God's image he made him; male and female he made them” (Genesis 1:27). So the meaning of “let us make” indicates that there is a co-creator, and it introduces one of equal address. For just as the Father who said “let us make a human being” is God, so also the one to whom he said “let us make” is God, since the deity of both persons is one—both the one who said, “Let us make a human being in God's image and in God's likeness,” and the one who made the human being. The voice “let us make” presents the all-holy and unvarying deity of the Father and the Son. For the image of God is simple and uncompounded, being fire in nature.

fixed: The first problem is not a mistranslation: the English already distinguishes the quoted 'our' in Genesis 1:26 from the narrator's 'God's' in Genesis 1:27, which matches the source's shift from first-person plural to third-person singular.

The second problem is not a mistranslation: the source says 'πῦρ οὔσα τῇ φύσει' (being fire in nature), and the English 'being light in nature' was an earlier attempted fix that did not satisfy the checkers; the correct rendering is 'being fire in nature'.
The third problem is a real awkwardness: 'equal address' has been changed to 'equal standing' to convey the sense of equal dignity or status.
